\begin{abstract}
Compute-governance regimes that restrict large training runs presuppose that a
regulator can tell when training happens on monitored hardware, and a power
meter outside the prover's control is the one passive channel available
against a prover who does not cooperate. We ask what such a meter can certify,
and answer with a ladder of four claims, each with a stated information cost
and a hard ceiling. Evidence comes from a literature-parameterized scenario
model of datacentre AI workloads and an explicit off-chip observation model,
against both a benign prover and an adaptive one who knows the detector. The
iteration cadence of synchronous training is recoverable by a tracked
cyclostationary detector, but the complete pipeline admits no analytic
calibration, so we report it as an effective score with per-trace surrogate
calibration rather than a constant false-alarm-rate test. Our central result
is the de-periodicisation frontier, which prices hiding against measured
throughput anchors and is strongly asymmetric: varying real work per iteration
hides from every fixed-frequency test at essentially zero cost, while the best
anchored attack against the tracking class buys little hiding for a $159\%$
overhead. Two limits are firmer than the detectors. The observation channel is
itself a condition on every claim --- a one-second-integrating, one-hertz
meter defeats all detectors on an honest workload --- and the meter certifies
a physical schedule, not training semantics: five non-training loads,
including one computing gradients and discarding them, are classified as
training by every rule we test. Escaping that ceiling means leaving the
passive channel for an active challenge protocol, which we specify but do not
run.
\end{abstract}

% ============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
% ============================================================================

Compute governance proposals call for evaluations, audits, and the
registration or prohibition of training runs above specified compute
thresholds
\citep{shavit2023chinchilla,sastry2024computing,baker2025verifying,heim2024thresholds};
U.S.~Executive Order 14110 briefly operationalised one such threshold,
requiring the reporting of training runs above $10^{26}$ FLOP
\citep{whitehouse2023eo14110}. Every such scheme presupposes that a regulator
can tell when training occurs on monitored hardware. Detection from
prover-owned telemetry is feasible but conditional on tamper-resistant read
paths that do not yet exist
\citep{rahman2026telemetry,ogara2025hardware}; active challenge-response
protocols remove the trust anchor but require the prover's participation
\citep{monfared2026timing}. A power meter outside the prover's control is the
one passive channel a verifier can read today against an uncooperative
prover. This paper asks, as a theory-and-methods question: what can such a
meter certify, with what methods, at what cost in verifier information, and
against an adversary who knows the detector?

The tools this requires are not new, and we do not claim them. Inferring which
activities are running from a single aggregate meter is the founding problem of
non-intrusive load monitoring \citep{hart1992nilm}, with three decades of
disaggregation technique behind it \citep{zoha2012nilm} and a power-side-channel
malware detector as its closest security-flavoured descendant
\citep{clark2013wattsupdoc}; certifying training from one datacentre meter is
that problem lifted from the household scale. Deciding whether a source is
active from noisy observations, explicitly against a transmitter trying to stay
below the detection floor, is the subject of spectrum sensing in cognitive
radio, whose canonical detector taxonomy --- the energy detector against the
matched filter against the cyclostationary feature detector, and the known
trade-offs between them --- is the structure of our own detector comparison
\citep{yucek2009spectrum}. And that computation is legible in power at all is
the founding premise of hardware-security power analysis, from differential
power analysis \citep{kocher1999dpa} and its correlation refinement
\citep{brier2004cpa} to profiled template attacks \citep{chari2002template},
with a parallel corpus attacking the inverse problem of recovering model
architecture or execution from GPU side channels
\citep{maia2022magnetic,naghibijouybari2018rendered,hu2020deepsniffer,liu2016codeexecution}.

What changes here is the question, the adversary, and the channel. Classical
load monitoring assumes cooperative or indifferent appliances and reads their
switching edges and steady-state signatures; side-channel analysis assumes a
proximate, high-bandwidth probe and a cooperative target running a known
computation, and extracts a fine-grained secret. We assume a remote, filtered,
low-rate meter and a target that actively hides, and we extract only the coarse
structural fact of whether efficient iteration-structured training is present.
The signature we exploit is accordingly neither a switching edge nor a
key-dependent transient but a quasi-periodic, frequency-wandering second-order
structure, which needs an order-tracking front end
\citep{dandawate1994cyclostationarity,bonnardot2005tacholess} that none of those
literatures supplies. The template-attack idea --- build a generative model of
the trace and test against it --- is nonetheless the honest precedent for the
optimality ceiling we benchmark our detectors against.

One literature does own the adversarial half of the problem. Pricing hiding
against detectability is formally the warden-versus-covert-transmitter game:
covert communication theory, from the square-root law of \citet{bash2013covert}
onward, and the information-theoretic model of steganography
\citep{cachin2004steganography}, which measures a stegosystem's security by the
relative entropy between cover and stego distributions, study exactly the
trade-off between how constrained a hidden activity is and how detectable it
remains. This is the literature that turns an empirical frontier into a
statement about \emph{every} verifier, by bounding a distributional distance
between the training-trace and null-trace laws as a function of the adversary's
distortion. Its existing results do not cover our object --- a
physics-constrained training schedule observed through a filtered, low-rate
meter --- so the bound is not inherited but has to be derived, which
\cref{subsec:identifiability} does for one attack family.

Our answer is that a passive external power trace can provide calibrated
structural evidence, and conditional evidence of efficient
iteration-structured training, but not universal semantic identification. An
adaptive prover can attack the exposed cadence, and the empirical question is
what detection--utility frontier erasing it requires. Stronger work
verification is possible only conditionally, on additional challenge and
transcript primitives.

That answer is not a single yes or no, so we do not organise the paper around a
single test. We organise it as a \emph{claim ladder} (\cref{tab:ladder}): four
claims of increasing governance relevance, each bought at a stated cost in
verifier information, and each with a hard ceiling that motivates the next.
Rung~1 establishes that order-coherent power structure is present, which is
evidence rather than identification. Rung~2 converts that structure into
training-likeness, at the price of committing to an inference null; its ceiling
is semantic non-identifiability. Rung~3 escapes both the null and that ceiling by
binding the physical response to an unpredictable challenge, at the price of the
prover's cooperation; its ceiling is a challenge-aware dummy load. Rung~4 ties
the response to declared work, but only given a transcript primitive we assume
rather than build. Each rung is the principled response to the previous rung's
ceiling, and part of the contribution is mapping the ladder honestly ---
including where each rung stops. The ladder is analogous in spirit to an
attestation ladder in which more verifier information permits a stronger claim at
greater institutional cost, but it is a ladder of claims and assumptions, not a
quantitative bound on unidentified compute. Within every rung we run two
adversary settings: a \textbf{benign} (non-adaptive) prover who runs its
workload without regard to the meter, and an \textbf{adaptive} (hiding) prover
who knows the detector and reshapes its schedule to evade it. Most of what is
interesting lies in the gap between them.

The body of the paper treats the two passive rungs, which is where the meter
alone can be made to do work. Rungs~3 and~4 leave the passive channel for an
active protocol --- authenticating a physical device by its response to an
unpredictable query, the premise of distance-bounding protocols
\citep{brands1994distance}, physical unclonable functions \citep{pappu2002puf},
and, in compute governance specifically, of challenge-response telemetry
\citep{monfared2026timing} --- and we specify that protocol without running it, in
\cref{app:active}.

Three restrictions fix the scope. First, the observable: we use the
time-resolved power trace and exclude the integrated-energy channel, so there is
no bounding of how much compute was performed and no energy-per-token pricing as
a verification instrument. This is a restriction on the observable, not a claim
that everything lives in the spectrum --- cyclostationary structure is expressed
spectrally, but the challenge correlation of Rung~3 is a time-domain operation on
the same trace. Second, the population: we do not claim a recoverable cadence is
universally necessary for training, and some conceivable execution can be made
fully aperiodic. We target instead efficient, synchronous, iteration-structured
training that exposes a recoverable cadence --- an expected physical signature of
that regime, especially where distributed synchronisation makes the modulation
deep and coherent. Destroying that cadence is then an adversarial action with a
measurable budget, not a counterexample to the method, and measuring that budget
is what \cref{sec:frontier} does.

The third restriction is the least comfortable, so we state it plainly: we do
not have hardware that can test the real question, and all the evidence here
lives on a synthetic generator. The iteration cadence exists on a single GPU,
and our measurements find the corresponding ripple at about $0.40\%$ of board
power, but a single saturated card has no communication phase, so the modulation
is shallow and easily washed out, and a single-node rig matches neither a
datacentre nor the aggregate regime of the workload model we adopt. The
generator (\cref{sec:scenario}) is therefore literature-parameterised, which we
are careful not to call calibrated: a factor of roughly $75$ separates the
modulation depth that model assumes from what we measure on one A100. Real
hardware enters as a negative transport case (\cref{sec:reality}), not as a
pillar, and the prediction that distributed synchronisation deepens and coheres
the signature is stated as falsifiable rather than claimed as a result.

The rest of the paper follows the physical chain. \Cref{sec:threat} fixes the
threat and measurement model, including the two things about this channel that
can be argued rather than measured: that no passive detector can identify
training semantics, and that hiding to a stated detectability must be paid for
in throughput or learning efficiency. \Cref{sec:scenario} gives the workload and
observation model that generates every number below. \Cref{sec:methods} develops
the detectors, \cref{sec:results} reports what they do, and \cref{sec:frontier}
prices what it costs an adaptive prover to defeat them. \Cref{sec:reality}
reports the one place we hold the model against measured hardware and it fails.
